summary:
Mato Grosso's 1989 Constitution, Article 10, item III, prohibits discrimination on grounds that include sexual orientation and obliges the state to implement measures ensuring no one is harmed or privileged on account of birth, race, colour, sex, marital status, nature of work, age, religion, sexual orientation, political or philosophical belief, disability, or any other particularity or condition. Gender identity is not named in that enumeration. A state decree published in the official gazette on 12 March 2021 guarantees travestis and trans people in Mato Grosso the right to use their social name before state public offices. The name is accepted on badges, cards and identification documents, state employees may register it in internal records and systems, and official publications are barred from using a person's civil name without consent.

Mato Grosso recorded 3 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the twelfth-highest raw count among Brazilian states in a national dossier that tallied 80 such killings across the country, and 43 killings of travestis, trans women, trans men, transmasculine and non-binary people in the state since 2017. These are raw counts. The source supplies no per-capita rate for Mato Grosso and no state homicide denominator, so the ranking reflects the size of the count rather than a measured level of risk against other states.

A jury in Mato Grosso sentenced businessman Jorlan Cristiano Ferreira, 44, to 13 years and 6 months in prison for the feminicide of trans woman Mayla, who was found dead with knife wounds in January 2024 on a farm beside MT-485 in Sorriso. He was also convicted of procedural fraud and concealment of a corpse. The jury found the killing was motivated by gender-based contempt and discrimination.

On 1 November 2025 a 39-year-old trans woman was expelled from a pizzeria in Feliz Natal after using the women's restroom, following complaints from staff and customers. The owner was taken to a police station for gender-identity discrimination and released on 2 November 2025 after a custody hearing subject to precautionary measures. The case was under judicial secrecy and Civil Police investigation, monitored by the Mato Grosso Public Prosecutor's Office, as of 16 September 2026.

Cuiabá prohibits trans athletes from women's sports. Councilman Beal Ranalli introduced a bill on 4 February 2025 to make biological sex the sole criterion for participation in city competitions; the City Council passed the prohibition on 19 August 2025, Mayor Abilio Brunini signed it, and it was published in the Official Gazette on 15 September 2025. The Mato Grosso LGBTQIA+ Pride Parade Association and the state Public Defender's Office sued to overturn it and sought 600,000 reais in damages for moral harm; the Court for Collective Actions dismissed the action on 30 October 2025, and the Association said it would appeal to the Court of Justice of Mato Grosso.

On 30 July 2025 Professor Maria Inês da Silva left the Municipal Conference of the Unified Health System in Cuiabá after Mayor Abilio Brunini interrupted her for using gender-neutral language. Health organisations, women's rights groups and Black rights organisations condemned the interruption.
tangentialFactors:
Mato Grosso's courts have repeatedly struck down local measures restricting discussion of gender and sexuality, and the pattern bears on the legal climate a visitor moves through rather than on any rule aimed at travellers. On 10 November 2022 the Mato Grosso Court of Justice granted preliminary relief holding unconstitutional a Sinop municipal law of March 2022 that prohibited the distribution, exhibition and dissemination of didactic material containing "gender ideology" in the city's public and private schools. The court found violation of the Federal Constitution and the Mato Grosso Constitution and an excess of municipal legislative competence; the action was brought by the Procuradoria-Geral de Justiça against the Sinop City Council with the participation of OAB-MT.

On 21 August 2026 the Órgão Especial of the Mato Grosso Court of Justice unanimously declared unconstitutional a state law sanctioned in April 2026 that prohibited teaching and dissemination in state public schools of content on so-called "gender ideology," gender identity and sexual orientation, including films, music, paintings and other artistic materials. The ruling voided the ban and restored schools' pedagogical autonomy to address gender identity and sexual orientation, on grounds of formal usurpation of the Union's exclusive competence over education guidelines under Article 22 of the Federal Constitution and violation of academic freedom, pluralism of ideas, and protection against bullying and discrimination.

On 4 February 2025 the same Cuiabá councilman, Beal Ranalli, introduced a separate bill to bar minors from the city's Pride events; the inventory records the introduction only, and its outcome is not established.
localsOnly:
For residents, the state's courts have been the main brake on municipal and state attempts to restrict gender content. The two rulings above cover the school curriculum in Sinop and across the state public school system. Whether the 2021 social-name decree binds private employers and businesses, as distinct from state public offices, is not stated in the source.

The Cuiabá prohibition on trans athletes in women's competitions applies to city-level sport, affecting local competitors and clubs; the challenge to it moved to the Court of Justice of Mato Grosso after the Court for Collective Actions dismissed the action on 30 October 2025, and the appeal was pending.

Mato Grosso's cumulative count of 43 killings of travestis, trans women, trans men, transmasculine and non-binary people between 2017 and 2025 is drawn from the same national dossier's per-state tabulation, which records raw counts without population denominators.
outOfScopeNotes:
The per-state figures for Mato Grosso carry no denominator. Neither the number of trans people living in the state nor the state's general homicide rate is given, so the 3 killings recorded for 2025 and the twelfth-place ranking cannot be read as a measure of risk above or below the background level of violence in the state. The national dossier is itself compiled from monitoring that its authors describe as incomplete.

Several matters are unresolved in the sources. The appeal against the Cuiabá sports prohibition had not been decided. The Feliz Natal restroom case remained under investigation and judicial secrecy with no recorded outcome. The outcome of the February 2025 bill to bar minors from Cuiabá Pride events is not recorded. No enforcement data on the 2021 social-name decree, and no record of how often its terms are refused by state offices, is available.
